title: Optimizing pollencounter for high throughput phenotyping of pollen quality in tomatoes
author: Ayenan, Danquah, et al.
materials: The optimized macro offers the opportunity to efficiently screen a large germplasm collection for pollen thermo-tolerance and selection of the best thermo-tolerant individuals in breeding programs. Increased efficiency in phenotyping can ultimately be translated into increased genetic gain [10].

Assessing pollen thermo-tolerance is important to identify thermo-tolerant genotypes. However, pollen can be viable but fail to germinate, which negatively affects fruits set. For this purpose, the percentage of germinated pollen could be a better indicator of thermo-tolerance. The current specifications of PollenCounter are not adapted to automatically assess the percentage of germinated pollen. Further improvement of the PollenCounter or development of other image-based phenotyping techniques to assess the percentage of pollen germination would improve the efficiency of the identification of new sources of thermo-tolerance in crops.

steps.title: Prepare modified Alexander stain
steps.instruction: Make the modified Alexander staining solution by mixing Malachite green, Orange G, acid Fuchsin, glycerol, acetic acid, distilled water and 95 % ethanol in the proportions described in reference [7].

steps.title: Harvest and slice anthers
steps.instruction: Select three to five newly opened flowers from the top of each genotype, remove sepals, petals and ovary, slice the anther and place the slice into a 1.5 ml Eppendorf tube.

steps.title: Stain pollen and release grains
steps.instruction: Add 40 µl of the Alexander stain to the sliced anther, vortex the tube for 20 seconds to release pollen, then pipette 10 µl of the stained suspension onto a pre‑heated microscope slide.

steps.title: Acquire high‑quality images
steps.instruction: View the slide with a Leica DM500 compound microscope using a 40× objective, ICC50 camera and Leica LAS software v2.1.0; capture three to four images per genotype at 2048 × 1536 px (31 images were used for macro optimisation).

steps.title: Run PollenCounter macro
steps.instruction: Open each image in ImageJ and execute the PollenCounter macro with the following parameters (Scenario S1): total‑pollen size 100–900 pixel², viable‑pollen size 100–900 pixel², circularity 0.4–1 for both channels. The macro will subtract background, split into red (total) and green (viable) channels, threshold to 8‑bit, dilate, fill holes, erode, apply watershed, count particles, and automatically save the results as a CSV file using the command saveAs("Results","/Directory/filename.csv").

substeps.instruction: Split image into red and green channels (saved automatically)
Convert each channel to binary (8‑bit) via thresholding
Dilate, fill holes and erode to clean particles
Apply watershed to separate clustered pollen grains
Count particles in red (total) and green (viable) channels
Save counts to a .csv file in the working directory

steps.title: Optional manual validation
steps.instruction: Manually count dark‑blue (viable) and light‑blue (dead) pollen grains on each image, record total and viable numbers, and compute viability percentage as PV = (Number of viable pollen / Total pollen) × 100.

steps.title: Apply good‑practice recommendations
steps.instruction: Follow these practices to maximise accuracy: gently pipette the stained suspension onto slides; let the pollen remain in stain for ~4 h before imaging; vortex thoroughly to avoid clumping; adjust camera contrast/brightness during acquisition or in ImageJ with run("Enhance Contrast…","saturated=xx") where xx is the desired saturation percentage; ensure high‑quality images without excess debris; verify that viable pollen appears dark‑blue (contrast too low under‑estimates total pollen and over‑estimates viability).

substeps.instruction: Gentle loading of 10 µl onto slide
Incubate slide in stain for about 4 hours
Adjust microscope camera settings for optimal contrast
If needed, use ImageJ contrast enhancement command with appropriate saturation
